1: # mcp-cpp-project-indexer
2: 
3: `mcp-cpp-project-indexer` is a deterministic C++ source-range indexer for
4: large, module-heavy projects and MCP-based AI code navigation.
5: 
6: It is not a compiler, LSP replacement, refactoring engine, semantic analyzer, or call-graph builder.
7: 
8: Its job is simple:
9: 
10: ```text
11: Find code. Read code. Do not guess code.
12: ```
13: 
14: The indexer maps C++ symbols, files, and C++20 modules to exact source ranges so an AI can read only the code it needs.
15: 
16: ---
17: 
18: ## 30-Second Overview
19: 
20: `mcp-cpp-project-indexer` builds a lightweight routing index over a C++ source
21: tree. MCP clients can then ask deterministic questions such as:
22: 
23: - where is this function/class/data member?
24: - which exact source range should be read?
25: - which module imports or exports this partition?
26: - which changed hunk intersects which indexed symbol or data range?
27: 
28: The indexer returns metadata and original source ranges. It does not claim to
29: understand the program. The AI still has to read the returned source and reason
30: from that evidence.
31: 
32: Minimal workflow:
33: 
34: ```text
35: User asks about Widget::OnScroll
36: -> find_symbol("Widget::OnScroll")
37: -> read_symbol(symbolId)
38: -> AI explains only what was visible in that source range
39: ```
40: 
41: This keeps large C++ projects out of the prompt until exact source evidence is
42: needed.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 5-Minute Quick Start
47: 
48: ### 1. Clone this repository
49: 
50: ```powershell
51: git clone https://github.com/walti1972/mcp-cpp-project-indexer.git
52: cd mcp-cpp-project-indexer
53: ```
54: 
55: ### 2. Build an index for your C++ project
56: 
57: ```powershell
58: python <indexer-root>\build_project_index.py `
59:   --root <project-root> `
60:   --output-root <project-root>\.mcp-cpp-project-indexer
61: ```
62: 
63: The generated index is written to:
64: 
65: ```text
66: <project-root>\.mcp-cpp-project-indexer
67: ```
68: 
69: ### 3. Start the MCP server
70: 
71: ```powershell
72: python <indexer-root>\code_index_mcp_server.py `
73:   --project-root <project-root> `
74:   --index-root <project-root>\.mcp-cpp-project-indexer
75: ```
76: 
77: For multiple MCP clients or a long-running shared process, use HTTP transport:
78: 
79: ```powershell
80: python <indexer-root>\code_index_mcp_server.py `
81:   --project-root <project-root> `
82:   --index-root <project-root>\.mcp-cpp-project-indexer `
83:   --transport http `
84:   --http-host 127.0.0.1 `
85:   --http-port 8765
86: ```
87: 
88: ### 4. Add the server to your MCP client
89: 
90: Minimal LM Studio-style config:
91: 
92: ```json
93: {
94:   "mcpServers": {
95:     "mcp-cpp-project-indexer": {
96:       "command": "python",
97:       "args": [
98:         "<indexer-root>\\code_index_mcp_server.py",
99:         "--project-root",
100:         "<project-root>",
101:         "--index-root",
102:         "<project-root>\\.mcp-cpp-project-indexer"
103:       ]
104:     }
105:   }
106: }
107: ```
108: 
109: ### 5. Ask for exact source, not whole files
110: 
111: Good first request:
112: 
113: ```text
114: Find the symbol Widget::OnScroll, read its implementation, and explain only
115: what is visible in the source range.
116: ```
117: 
118: Expected tool path:
119: 
120: ```text
121: find_symbol -> read_symbol -> source-grounded answer
122: ```
123: 
124: For best results, give your AI the rules from
125: [prompt_template.md](prompt_template.md). The short version is:
126: 
127: ```text
128: Use metadata to locate code. Read exact source ranges before explaining behavior.
129: Do not infer implementation behavior from metadata alone.
130: ```
131: 
132: ---
133:

160: 
161: ## 🚀 Production Scale & Performance
162: 
163: This project is used on real C++ codebases, not only toy examples. Two recent
164: scale runs show the intended range:
165: 
166: | Project | Files | Source lines | Lexer tokens | Symbols | Data declarations | C++20 modules | Full build |
167: |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
168: | Anonymized commercial C++20 project | 7,046 | 979,658 | 4,682,882 | 97,924 | 36,551 | 3,754 | 19.5s |
169: | Chromium checkout | 137,622 | 30,792,607 | 137,365,399 | 2,327,255 | 818,188 | 0 | ~24m 32s |
170: 
171: These numbers are machine-dependent. The Chromium run used `--jobs 60` on a
172: high-core workstation with an Intel Xeon Silver 4316 system, 128 GB RAM, and
173: enterprise NVMe SSD storage. It is a useful public stress test because it
174: exercises a very large classic include-based C++ codebase, while the anonymized
175: commercial project exercises dense C++20 module and partition metadata. The
176: Chromium run also validated the data/member indexer at scale: after fixing
177: nested-template `>>` depth handling, the public stress test surfaced **46,529**
178: additional data declarations and **66,866** additional data-name aliases.
179: 
180: The SQLite-backed lookup index keeps server startup practical even at Chromium
181: scale: the MCP server can start immediately and stay around **200 MB RAM** after
182: startup instead of loading millions of symbol/data/name entries into Python
183: objects.
184: 
185: It is designed for workflows that combine the Codex desktop app or other MCP
186: clients with Visual Studio navigation and, when needed, binary/decompiler
187: evidence from tools such as IDA Pro.
188: 
189: In one measured workflow, exact source-range routing reduced source text read
190: from roughly 2,000 lines to 283 lines, an **86% reduction**.
191: 
192: ---
193: 
194: ## TUI Control Center
195: 
196: For daily use, the indexer includes an optional mouse-capable TUI. It turns the
197: project index into a small local control center:
198: 
199: - start the HTTP MCP server and watcher from one place
200: - run full builds, incremental updates, fast updates, and module-map rebuilds
201: - watch live server, watcher, lock, process, token, and index stats
202: - inspect build/update logs without switching tools
203: - toggle diagnostic file sections for deeper parser evidence when needed
204: 
205: ![TUI control center](docs/assets/tui-control-center.svg)
206: 
207: Install the optional UI dependency and start the control center with explicit
208: project/index paths:
209: 
210: ```powershell
211: pip install -r <indexer-root>\requirements-ui.txt
212: 
213: python <indexer-root>\indexer_tui.py `
214:   --root <project-root> `
215:   --index-root <project-root>\.mcp-cpp-project-indexer `
216:   --jobs 20 `
217:   --http-url http://127.0.0.1:8765
218: ```
219:

1: # MIRCV's project: SEPP (Search Engine ++)
2: 
3: ![](https://github.com/scarburato/searchenginepp/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)
4: 
5: A C++ program that creates an inverted index structure from a set of text documents and a program that processes queries over such inverted index.
6: 
7: 📖 Report avaibile here: [report.pdf](report.pdf) 
8: 
9: ## Clone the Repository
10: 
11: To clone the repository, use the following command:
12: 
13: ```bash
14: git clone --recursive https://github.com/scarburato/searchenginepp.git
15: ```
16: 
17: ## Dependencies
18: 
19: ### Ubuntu
20: 
21: To ensure the program works on Ubuntu, make sure you have the following dependencies installed:
22: 
23: ```bash
24: sudo apt-get update
25: sudo apt install build-essential cmake libstemmer-dev libhyperscan-dev
26: ```
27: 
28: If you're not building on an amd64 (x86) system you may have to install `vectorscan` in place of `hyperscan`, on Ubuntu
29: the package to install should be named `libvectorscan-dev`.
30: 
31: ### MacOS
32: 
33: Assuming you have already installed a C++ compiler and the [brew packet manager](https://formulae.brew.sh/); to compile
34: on MacOS, you need to install the following dependencies:
35: 
36: ```shell
37: brew install cmake snowball hyperscan
38: ```
39: 
40: If you're not building on an amd64 (x86) system, you have to install `vectorscan` in place of `hyperscan`.
41: 
42: The `CMakeLists.txt` file assumes that brew installs its stuff in `$(brew --prefix)`, if your version of brew differs
43: then modify the `CMakeLists.txt` file accordingly.
44: 
45: ## Build
46: 
47: Navigate to the project directory and use the following commands:
48: 
49: ```bash
50: mkdir build
51: cd build/
52: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DUSE_STEMMER:BOOL=ON -DFIX_MSMARCO_LATIN1:BOOL=ON -DTEXT_FULL_LATIN1_CASE:BOOL=ON ..
53: make -j8
54: ```
55: 
56: you should replace the `-j8` flag with the number of cores in your CPU.
57: 
58: On MacOS, if perfidious Apple's clang gives you problems compiling, you should consider installing GNU GCC or a more
59: recent version of clang through brew.
60: 
61: ### CMake options
62: 
63: Those are the building options:
64: 
65: - `USE_STEMMER` used to enable or disable Snowball's stemmer and stopword removal
66: - `FIX_MSMARCO_LATIN1` used to enable or disable heuristic and encoding fix for certain wronly encoded docs in MSMARCO. If you are not using MSMARCO you should put this flag to OFF (default option is OFF)
67: - `TEXT_FULL_LATIN1_CASE` replaces the ASCII-only lower-case algorithm with a latin1 (a larger subset of utf8) lower-case
68: - `USE_FAST_LOG` replaces the floating point version of log with a faster integer version. It doesn't improve performance by much
69: 
70: ### Run tests
71: 
72: Go in the `build/` directory and use the following command:
73: 
74: ```bash
75: tests/Google_Tests_run
76: ```
77: 
78: If all tests return RUN OK, it means all tests passed successfully.
79: 
80: ## Build the Index
81: 
82: To read the collection efficiently, use the following command:
83: 
84: ```bash
85: time tar -xOzf ../data/collection.tar.gz collection.tsv | ./builder
86: ```
87: 
88: On MacOS, you may find that GNU's implementation of `tar` is faster; you can install it with brew 
89: --- `brew install gnu-tar` --- and then replace `tar` with `gtar` in the command above.
90: 
91: The use of `tar` alongside UNIX's pipes, allows the system to decompress the collection
92: in blocks, and keep in the input buffer of only the chunk that's being proccessed at the moment,

226: ## 💡 Why This Tool?
227: 
228: Large C++ projects are expensive to feed into an AI model when entire files are
229: loaded just to find one function, class, import, or declaration. C++20 modules
230: make this harder: many IDE/LSP-style tools still struggle with large module
231: graphs, partitions, generated SDK headers, and build-specific configuration.
232: 
233: This indexer solves a narrower but very practical problem: it gives the AI a
234: small, deterministic routing map. The AI can locate the relevant symbol,
235: module, file, or changed hunk first, then read only the exact original source
236: lines needed for the task.
